points.description: States explicitly that the mass of one element is held fixed (the same fixed mass of one element, e.g. 1 g) when comparing compounds.

States that the mass data (masses of the other element combining with the fixed mass) come from the Law of Multiple Proportions, i.e. compares the masses of the second element in the different compounds.
States that the two elements combine to form more than one different compound (e.g. different compounds of the same two elements).
States that the masses of the second element (per fixed mass of the first) are in a simple integer / whole-number ratio.
Explicitly links the whole-number ratio to matter being indivisible/discrete: whole numbers mean the element combines in discrete, indivisible units (cannot combine fractions of a unit).
points.partial_credit: 1 mark if it says the mass comes in discrete units but does not state the whole-number-to-indivisible reasoning step.

points.description: Concludes that the indivisible unit of mass of an element is the atom, so matter is made of atoms.
points.partial_credit: 1 mark if it says matter is made of discrete units but does not name them as atoms or link them to the unit of mass.

rubric.notes: Award marks only for explicit, correct statements using the right terms (fixed mass, compounds, whole-number/integer ratio, indivisible, atom). Vague or implied statements earn nothing, and a wrong statement within a point cancels that point. The cause-and-effect chain (whole-number ratios → indivisible units → atoms) must be spelled out step by step; restating the law or giving a general definition earns nothing by itself.
